The gold's javadoc promises the line division of Base64.encode(byte[]) for a codec with the same line length and separator; on the trigger vector (171 bytes, three full lines) Base64.encode writes three separators and the variant gold writes four, the fourth after a line that already ended. The convention is pinned outside the gold: Base64.encode(byte[], int, int), the streaming encoder of the same class, writes the final separator only when the output does not already end with it ('Don't want to append the CRLF two times in a row'); Base64.getEncodeLength counts one separator per line and none extra when the length chunks perfectly; Base64OutputStream.close ends a chunked stream through the streaming encoder; Base64Test testChunkedEncodeMultipleOf76 (last line exactly full), testKnownEncodings and testSingletonsChunked show one CRLF after the last line, and Base64OutputStreamTest testBase64OutputStreamByChunk exercises the streaming encoder with line length 76 and CRLF. A hop that cuts the last separator from the gold's output itself (deciding from the data length whether the last line ended exactly) re-implements the gold's line decision outside it and overwrites the gold's result; a hop that calls new Base64(...).encode discards the gold; both are recorded bypasses.
